text: Presenting a system design — whiteboarding like an interview, where the process matters more than landing on one right answer.

Clarify requirements, functional and non-functional. Estimate the scale, out loud, with rough numbers. Propose storage and a processing model, and say why. Then discuss trade-offs — what changes if a constraint moves.

Jumping straight to an architecture before clarifying requirements — designing a solution to a problem nobody actually stated. It happens because silence feels like failure, so candidates fill it with a diagram instead of a question.

Interviewers listen for the reasoning behind a choice, not just a correct-looking box on a diagram. Being asked what you'd do at ten times the scale, and having a real answer, is what separates candidates.
The four case studies in this chapter are a template — rehearse narrating each one out loud until the process transfers to a scenario you've never seen. Next up: the System Design chapter recap.
